13.8 As regards construction of fencing 150 yards away from the Border is concerned, the
Home Secretary has stated that there are certain areas where certain difficulties are being
experienced. The general proposition is that the fencing would be 150 yards away from the Border.
In this regard, the Government was facing problems from both the sides. Some State Governments
have objected to this because on the other side of the fencing, there are orchards and farming,
and in some areas, people are also residing. In many of the areas, this 150 yards is closer to the
Border where objection has been raised by Bangladesh Rifles. The Home Secretary explaining the
reason for this condition of 150 yards away from the Border stated that there was an unsigned
agreement since 1975 between Bangladesh and India. The unsigned agreement was that for 150
yards, there would be no defence structure. Though ‘fencing’ is not a defence structure,
Bangladesh has been insisting that India cannot build even fencing within 150 yards of the Border.
It was also agreed that because of this condition, a large number of villages and cultivable land
are there on the other side of the fence. Gates are also there which are opened as frequently as
possible.
13.9 The Committee is very much concerned about the problems being faced by the people
residing at the Border areas. It is a fact that there are properties of the Border people
where agricultural activities are carried out and in some areas, people are also residing in
this 150-yard of area. The Committee is anguished to note that people face lot of problems
under the current dispensation and no solution has been found so far for this problem. The
Committee recommends that the Government may hold discussion with Bangladesh in
consultation with the Ministry of External Affairs for a settlement of the problem. In
consultation with all concerned, the fencing may be taken nearer to the border instead of
150 yards away from the border. In case it is not possible the Government may buy the land
within this 150-yard of the Border so that the people who have properties within the 150
yards may not face problems anymore. The Ministry of Home Affairs may hold discussions
with all concerned, including the Ministry of External Affairs and find a permanent solution
at the earliest.
NAXALISM
14. Naxalism besides being a law and order problem, has deep socio-economic dimensions. The
Central Government has taken measures to address the problem simultaneously on security,

25
development and public perception management fronts. Those measures include deployment of
CPMFs to assist the State Police, sharing of actionable intelligence by central security agencies,
sanction of India Reserve Battalions and financial assistance for modernising and equipping of the
State Police forces.
14.1 The Ministry have stated that Rs. 4173.71 crore has been provided to the naxal affected
States, under the Police Modernisation Fund assistance. In addition, Rs. 210.68 crore has been
given as reimbursement of Security Related Expenditure. On the developmental front, assistance to
the order of Rs. 1597.60 crore has been given under the Backward Districts Initiative (BDI)
Scheme, during last 4 years, Naxal situation in the country is being monitored at various levels in
the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Ministry have also stated that a multi-pronged strategy
essentially of sustained and effective police action coupled with accelerated socio-economic
development and management of public perception is being pursued to effectively tackle the naxalite
menace.
14.2 The Ministry in its written reply to the questionnaire has inter-alia furnished details of
monitoring mechanism which have been set up by the Government for tackling Naxalism which
includes a periodical review by the Cabinet Committee on Security on naxal situation, constitution
of a Standing Committee of the Chief Ministers of the naxal affected States chaired by the Union
Home Minister, Quarterly Coordination Centre meetings chaired by the Union Home Secretary with
the Chief Secretaries and the Directors General of Police of the affected States and the monthly
Task Force meetings of Nodal Officers of naxal affected States and Central agencies taken by
Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs. The States have also been asked to hold a monthly
review by the DGP and the bi-monthly review by the Chief Secretary of the naxal situation and
the measures and stratagies to contain the naxal problem on both security and development fronts.
14.3 The Home Secretary during the course of his presentation stated that a number of steps
were being taken by the Ministry for tackling naxal violence effectively. He stated that there had
been a decline in the overall level of violence. In a number of States the decline has been quite
significant. He also explained that the programme of the Government of India, included deployment
of Central Para-Military Forces in the Naxalite areas on a no-cost basis to the States. Special
Security Related Expenditure in the context of the Police Modernisation Schemes, enabling the
States to upgrade their weaponry, additional IR battalions had been sanctioned for the naxal-
affected States. Specialised training in guerilla warfare had also been provided to the police
personnel in the army and the CPMF training centres. Mine-protected vehicles and other
surveillance equipments have been supplied to them. Forty per cent recruitment in the Central
Paramilitary Forces was expected to be from the border areas and areas affected by militancy with
the aim of providing employment.
14.4 The Home Secretary however informed the Committee that some of the naxal affected
States do not found to have sufficient force system. Certain States have a large number of
vacancies in their force. One of the State has about 10,000 vacancies. He further stated that there
is a limit upto which the CPMFs can help the States forces but they can not completely substitute
the State Police Forces and the Ministry was impressing upon the States to fill up the vacancies
on priority basis. The Home Secretary has also stated that the States Police Forces in many cases
do not follow the Standred Operating Procedure (SOP) which results in easy attack by the naxals.
14.5 The Committee notes that the Government are taking steps on different fronts
including the developmental efforts. The Committee has also recommended in successive
reports for a holistic approach in tackling the naxal problem. The Committee however, feels
that there is no perceptible change on the socio-economic front. Though the socio-economic
development cannot be quantified, it can be perceived and if such a perceptible change is
there, undoubtedly it will have a lasting impact. The Committee reiterating the earlier

26
recommendation that an effective developmental approach may be adopted, further
recommends that various schemes under the Ministries of Rural Development and other
Ministries may also be implemented for the socio-economic development in the naxal
affected areas. There needs to be an effective monitoring mechanism on the implementation
of these schemes with the involvement of all the concerned Ministries and agencies.
14.6 The Committee also reiterates its observation made earlier that the naxal problem
is no longer a problem of a few States. It has acquired a national dimension posing gravest
threat to the national security. The naxal activities have spread to more than twelve States
and are reported to be having links with external agencies including ISI. The Committee
is therefore, of the considered view that taking into account the growth and influence of
the Naxal groups in several States and the grave threat posed by it to the internal security
of the country, it is high time that the Ministry constitute a Unified Command to
effectively tackle the menace. Besides the Central Paramilitary Forces, State Police Forces
may also contribute to the unified command. The Committee also takes note of the
observation made by the Home Secretary that naxal attacks on several occasions take place
due to non observance of ‘Standard Operating Procedure’ (SOP) by the State police forces.
The Committee therefore, strongly recommends that Government may consider creating a
unified command common to all the naxal affected States.
14.7 One of the Members of the Committee mentioned that private sector industries are suffering
on many counts due to the naxal threats in affected areas. Public Sector Undertakings are provided
security by the Central Industrial Security Force whereas the private sector industries have to make
their own security arrangements. The private security arrangement by the industries is not adequate
enough to tackle the naxal threats. The Home Secretary replying to this, during the course of the
oral evidence, stated that if any private sector organization in the affected area wants to be armed
sufficiently to protect itself, applications can be made by them for licence or any kind of
protection which can be examined on case-by-case basis. He further assured the Committee to look
into the matter.
14.8 The Committee agrees that naxal threat is a big menace for any industry, including
the private sector. The issue needs to be examined to see that private sector industries are
also protected in the naxal-affected areas. The Ministry of Home Affairs may examine the
matter in consultation with all concerned and take an early decision.
MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCES
15. The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for Modernization
of State Police Forces since 1969-70 to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in
modernizing their forces. The Scheme provided assistance to the State Governments, as 50% grant-
in-aid and 50% loans for purchase of vehicles, equipments for forensic science labs, fingerprint
bureau, police training, weaponry, construction of housing for police personnel, police stations,
training buildings etc. Equal matching contributions was expected from the State Governments.
15.1 To face multifarious challenges including controlling law and order, maintaining internal
security, on account of insurgency/extremism/terrorism in some of the States, the Central
Government considered it necessary to modernize the State Police Forces quickly, and therefore,
the Annual Central Assistance under the scheme was enhanced to Rs.1000 crore from year
2000-01, and thereafter to Rs.1400 crore in 2003-04. While enhancing the Annual Central Allocation
during 2003-04, it was also decided to provide the entire Central assistance as grant-in-aid. During
the Financial Year 2005-06, the Government has further enhanced the allocation to RS.1645.00
crore with specific focus on States facing problems of terrorism, left-wing extremism, etc. In a
decision taken in September, 2005, 100% Central funding is provided for NE States and J&K and
75% Central funding for the remaining 20 States.

27
15.2 The Committee in its 119th Report had recommended to extend this important scheme to
UTs also and further recommended to make necessary allocation at RE stage in 2006-07. As a
result, a provision of Rs. 40 crore was made for the modernization of Police Forces in UTs at
RE stage for 2006-07.
15.3 For the year 2007-08, an a mount of Rs. 1190.63 crore has been allocated under this head
against the projection of Rs. 1921.80 crore. Out of which Rs. 1013.83 crore is provided
as assistance to States for modernisation of Police in States whereas Rs. 41.20 crore and
Rs. 13.20 crore are provided to UTs without legislature and UTs with legislature, respectively.
Rs. 122.40, crore have been provided for assistance to Delhi Police for modernization.
15.4 The Ministry have informed the Committee that a mid-term evaluation of the Modernization
of State Police Forces Scheme was conducted by Bureau of Police Research and Development
(BPR&D) in the year 2006. The performance of the States under this scheme has been analyzed
through evaluation of utilization of funds for modernization made available to them. The general
trend in the expenditure of modernization funds in different States varies with the fixation of
priority on different areas of modernization. Overall, it has been observed that more than 50% fund
is utilized in the police housing and police buildings activities; around 20% for police mobility, 1-6%
for police training, 2-13% for police weaponry etc.
15.5 The Ministry have also stated that the State Governments are pursued vigorously for better
and full utilization of funds. Emphasis is also laid on equipping the police forces on a balanced
scale, for which all State plans formulated by them are considered and approved by the High
Powered Committee constituted by the Ministry. The plans are formulated by the respective States
on the basis of their urgent local needs.
15.6 The Committee takes note of the Mid-Term evaluation of the Modernisation of State
Police Forces Scheme by BPR&D. One of the findings made by the BPR&D in the study
which causes concern to the Committee is that more than 50 per cent of the fund is utilized
in the police housing and police building activities. The Committee is of the view that with
the new technological advances taking place in a feverish pitch and in view of the fact that
the Police Forces in India function with age-old equipments and gadgets, much of the
scheme of modernization should concentrate on providing modern gadgets, improving
technology, providing IT facilities, etc. Spending more than 50 per cent on building activities
defeats the very purpose of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends
that the Ministry of Home Affairs may review the scheme in the light of pattern of
expenditure incurred by the States and prepare a list of activities which should lay thrust
on improving technology and providing modern gadgets, etc.
15.7 The Committee is constrained to note that there was an unspent balance of
Rs. 47.81 crore under the Scheme of Modernisation of Police forces as on 31.12.2006.
Though the Ministry have stated that they are pursuing vigorously with the States for better
and full utilization of funds, the Committee desires that they may lay a condition stating
that further funds would be released only after the full expenditure of the previous balance.
It should be insisted upon all the States to send Utilisation Certificates and receipt thereof
may also be put as one of the conditions for further release of funds. These are necessary
to ensure that States spend the funds meant for Modernization of Police Forces in a better
manner and as per the schedule.
15.8 In regard to the Scheme for Modemisation of Police Forces in Union Territories; the
Ministry have stated that each UT is required to prepare an Annual Action Plan and get it approved
by the Committee constituted in the Ministry of Home Affairs for this purpose. Accordingly, the
UTs had submitted their Annual Action Plans for 2006-07, which were considered and approved

28
by the Committee with certain modifications, and they were advised to initiate action for
implementation thereof.
15.9 The Ministry have also stated that while communicating approval for implementation of
Annual Action Plans, the Union Territories were also advised that expenditure on the Plan for
2006-07 would be met by locating savings within the sanctioned budget grant. In case it was not
found possible to adjust the amount within the sanctioned grant, they would submit proposals for
sanction of additional funds at RE stage. Since most of the UTs could not find savings, additional
funds to the tune of Rs. 40 crores had been provided in RE 2006-07 through re-appropriation.
15.10 The Committee notes with satisfaction launching of the scheme of Modernisation of
Police Forces in UTs. Since it was initiated in 2006-07 only, it would be too early to assess
the scheme. The Committee notes that UTs were asked in 2006-07 to implement this
scheme effectively by having savings. Though ultimately additional allocation had to be
made as UTs could not effect savings, such a situation could have been avoided by making
allocation initially which would have enabled the UTs to start implementation immediately.
The Ministry may therefore from time-to-time monitor the implementation of the scheme
and ensure that the physical as well as financial target are achieved in time by the State
and Union Territories.
15.11 The Committee is given to understand that Special Branches in States/UTs Police
Forces play an important role in collection of intelligence through technical surveillance and
the real and actionable intelligence at the micro-level comes through human assets.
However, the Committee is of the view that the Special Branches neither have sufficient
infrastructure nor modern equipment and gadgets, etc. In view of the current internal
security situation and the growing naxalite and terrorist activities, strengthening and
modernization of Special Branches acquire significance. The Committee, therefore, feels
that the Special Branches in the States/Union Territories Police Forces need to be revamped
by enhancing their manpower by way of filling up of vacancies; posting of competent officers
with reasonable tenure, dedicated staff for intelligence work right up to the police station
level and reactivating beat constable system and above all making available modern
equipment and gadgets for interception and special training for personnel posted therein.
15.12 The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may
impress upon the State/Union Territories Governments/Administrations to strengthen their
Special Branches. The Ministry may also allocate some of the funds under Modernization of
States Police Forces Scheme for strengthening and modernization of Special Branches.
MODERNISATION OF PRISON ADMINISTRATION
16. The Central Government in 2002-03 launched a non-plan scheme for construction of
additional jails to reduce overcrowding, repair and renovation of existing jails, improvement in
sanitation and water supply and construction of living accommodation for prisons staff. The
scheme known as the Modernization of Prisons is being implemented in 27 States over a period
of five years (2002-07) with an outlay of Rs. 1800 crore. The cost is being shared between Central
Government and State Governments in the ratio of 75:25 respectively.
16.1 The Ministry have stated that though this scheme was launched in 2002-03, the Central
share was released to the States only in March 2003. The State Governments were granted eighteen
months from the date of release to utilize the amounts released to them. Further, there were several
teething problems in the States at the beginning of the scheme and many of them could not utilize
the amount promptly. Due to this, the Scheme has since been extended by a period of two years
w.e.f. 1.4.2007 without affecting the total outlay of Rs. 1800 crore.

29
16.2 This scheme has four components. The physical progress of each component for 2006-07
is as under, as submitted by the Ministry:
“Construction of New Jail:  The Central Empowered Committee has so far approved
the construction of 163 jails of different categories in various States. Out of this, 99 jails
are expected to be completed by 31.3.2007. Targets for 2007-08 and 2008-09 are
construction of 50 jails and 8 jails respectively.
Repairs and Renovations and expansion of jails:  Under this head State Governments
are taking up work for repairs and renovations of the existing jails, which are in dilapidated
condition. The Central Empowered Committee has approved construction of 1360 additional
barracks in the existing jails to augment the capacity in jails. Out of this, 935 additional
barracks are expected to be completed by 31.3.2007. Targets for 2007-08 and 2008-09
are fixed at construction of 305 and 120 barrels respectively.
Construction of Staff Quarters: Construction of 8573 quarters of different categories
for prison personnel has so far been approved. Out of this, 6363 staff quarters are expected
to be completed by 31.3.2007. Targets for 2007-08 and 2008-09 are fixed at construction
of 1735 and 3210 staff quarters respectively.
Water and Sanitation:  Under this head, State Governments were required to take up
various works for providing water and sanitation facilities for prisoners and prison
personnel in various jails. It was required to construct overhead tanks for drinking water,
construction of toilets, drainage and sanitation work. All these works are under various
stages of completion.”
16.3 The Committee was informed that the release to the State Governments were made on the
basis of their performances. Due to this reason, the full central share could not be released against
the annual plans of 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07 to all States. However, majority of
States were now performing well and the total amount spent by the State Government upto
31.12.2006 was Rs. 967.89 crore against the central assistance of Rs. 1016.17 crore. The
percentage of utilisation vis a vis  the central share is 95%.
16.4 On a query whether there is any perceptible change in the condition of inmates in the Indian
prisons after the scheme has been launched and whether any study has been conducted to evaluate
the same the Ministry have stated as under:
“The scheme would definitely help in improving the physical condition in prison as
creation of additional accommodation would help in reducing overcrowding. Repairs,
renovation and water and sanitation works will help in improving the living condition of
prisoners. The construction of staff quarters for prisons personnel will boost the morale of
the prison staff which will thereby help them in performing their duty more efficiently.
A study/evaluation is normally carried out after the completion of the scheme.
However the scheme is closely monitored and review meetings are held regularly at senior
levels. The feedback in their meetings from the States has been positive. The officials of
the Ministry of Home Affairs have been visiting the States regularly to monitor the progress
of the scheme and the feedback received is that the scheme is proving to be extremely
useful and will go a long way in improving the condition of prisoners in jails”
16.5 The Committee reiterates its observation made in its 119th Report that the Scheme,
if implemented in the right earnest, would go a long way in improving the conditions in the
prisons and the inmates thereof. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that more
emphasis is laid under the Scheme on the construction work, repairs and renovation than
improving the actual conditions inside the jails for the prisoners. The Committee, therefore,

30
strongly recommends that the Government may redesign the guidelines for the scheme
laying more emphasis on improving the facilities/conditions of the prisoners.
16.6 The Committee also expresses its concern that even though the Scheme started in
2002-2003, no evaluation of its performance has been made so far. The Ministry’s reply that
a study evaluation is normally carried out after completion of the scheme shows a casual
approach of dealing with the matter. Whenever any scheme is launched a mid-term
evaluation is carried out. Since the scheme has been extended by two more years with effect
from 01.04.2007, the Government may conduct a mid-term evaluation immediately to assess
its efficacy.
16.7 The Committee is presently examining the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment)
Bill, 2006. One of the provisions in the Bill seeks to amend Section 167 of the Code for
allowing video conferencing between the Jail and the Court for trial of an accused to avoid
transportation of the accused to the court. To make this provision workable it is essential
to modernise the jails, especially enabling those with IT facilities, computers and all related
equipments. Most of the jails in the country do not have this facility at present. In case,
the above-mentioned amendment is enacted, it would practically be of no use unless the
required infrastructure is available in the jails. The Committee therefore, recommends that
creation of infrastructure in the jails for enabling video linkages between the jails and the
courts, may be made part of the scheme of Modernisation of Prisons and if necessary a
separate allocation may be made for that purpose.

REPEALING OF OBSOLETE ACTS
18. It was brought to the notice of Committee by some of its Members that the Ministry of
Home Affairs is administering reveral laws of pre-independence era like the Explosives Substances
Act, 1908; the Passport Entry into India Act, 1920; Official Secrets Act, 1923; Registration of
Foreigners’ Act, 1939; Foreigners Act, 1936, etc. Six decades have passed since the country got
independence. It is therefore high time that these Act need to be reviewed keeping in view the
changing needs of the society and the present day ground realities.
18.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may have a fresh look at
these laws and bring them in line with the present times. The Committee also recommends
that the obsolete laws need to be repealed from time to time and this should be
appropriately included in the Action Plan of the Ministry.

ACQUIRING OF WEAPONS BY SPORTSPERSONS
19. One of the Members of the Committee raised a point relating to the problems faced by
sportspersons in acquiring imported weapons. He has also mentioned that a proposal in this regard
from the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has been pending with the Ministry of Home Affairs.
19.1 Responding to the issue, the Home Secretary submitted that proposals for giving certain
facilities were forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs when he was Secretary, Ministry of
Youth Affairs and Sports. He also assured that the matter would be looked into.
19.2 The Ministry, in the written reply, stated that a suggestion was received earlier to expand
the definition of a ‘renowned shooter’, in the context of National Shooting Championship. The
suggestion had already been considered in MHA in consultation with Ministry of Youth Affairs and
Sports, National Rifle Association of India (NRAI) and Sports Authority of India (SAI). The
Ministry further stated that another suggestion was received later about ‘wild card entrants’
advising to take safeguards so that the facilities of a ‘renowned shooter’ are not mis-utilised by
wild card entrants. The Ministry have also stated that the new points raised require examination
afresh and a reference has been made to the authorities concerned on 5.4.2007.
19.3 The Committee feels that use of advanced and imported weapons is essential for
shooters who participate in national and international championships. To enable the shooters
to excel in international events, it is necessary for the Government to allow them to import
advanced weapons. The Government may consider all the aspects relating to permission for
acquiring of imported weapons by the shooters and take an early decision in the matter. The
Committee also suggests that the sportspersons, so permitted to acquire imported weapons,
may also be permitted to dispose them of after every three years as the use of the weapons
may involve wear and tear and technological changes may make it obsolete.

21.3 The Finance Secretary of the U.T. of Chandigarh during the course of his oral evidence
expressed satisfaction with budget allocations and added that whenever the UT required funds it
was provided it. On the issue of slum rehabilitation, he informed the Committee that the
Administration has set up ten rehabilitation colonies where 30,000 families have been rehabilitated.
He further informed the Committee that presently, the Chandigarh Administration has got a
biometric survey done and identified about 23,841 families which have encroached upon 200 acres
of precious land owned by the administration. He informed the Committee that some of the people
who were given ownership, have sold their tenements and houses and again encroached upon the
Government land. In view of this, a scheme has been devised to construct 25,000 one-room flats
and to give the people on rent for Rs. 800 per month. Land has already been acquired for this
purpose. Such colonies would be provided with medical centres, schools, community centres,
vocational training centres, adequate parks, temples and gurudwaras etc. The Government of India,
under the Jawaharlal Renewal Mission Programme has already sanctioned Rs. 400 crores for this
purpose.
21.4 On the issue of Chandigarh Technology Park, the Finance Secretary informed the
Committee that Chandigarh is the only place in the north of the country where this project was
conceived in 2002. There were three types of sites which were earmarked in the project. One was
the main campus site, the second was the mini campus site, and the third was the built to suit
site with different kinds of area. To begin with, two companies i.e. DLF and Infosys came to
Chandigarh. DLF constructed about 6 lakh square feet office area for IT companies over twelve
and a half acres of land. Infosys Technology were allotted 20 acres of land, to begin with, and
another 10 acre of land would be allotted later. Infosys has constructed 5,25,000 square feet
and they have started operating from this campus. About 1,000 engineers have already started

41
working from the Chandigarh technology centre. About 7 to 8 companies have occupied space in
DLF building and about 2,000 people have started working from the DLF premises. He also stated
that land has been allotted to several other companies and so far, the private sector has invested
about Rs. 250 crores in this project. The Chandigarh administration had laid the basic services. The
present area of the Technology Park is 237 acres. 112 acres have been declared a Special
Economic Zone for Information Technology. It has been notified also. The remaining 125 acres
have been approved as SEZ, but not yet notified. Another 260 acres of land is being added to the
Chandigarh Technology Park because there are a large number of companies which are on the
waiting list and have been requesting UT administration for allotment of land. The Finance
Secretary has further stated that the UT has set up a Technology Habitat in partnership with the
private sector where about 2500 residential flats are coming up for the people who would be
working in this Technology Park. The whole idea was that people need not travel much distance.
They should stay closer to the place. The Chandigarh Technology Park has been a big success and
at the end of it, it would generate employment for 40,000 people, he added.
21.5 W ith regard to building bye-laws, the Finance Secretary informed the Committee that
Chandigarh Administration is following a very stringent bye laws and that is the reason that
Chandigarh has been able to remain as it is today. So far, 80 notifications have been issued on the
basis of representations received from residents of various areas and accordingly building bye laws
have been amended to strike a balance between the planned character of the city and the reasonable
requests of the residents. The Finance Secretary further informed the Committee that after its visit
to the UT in 2005, a Committee of local representatives was constituted which made certain
recommendations. The UT administration examined those recommendations and accepted many of
them. There were two major demands made by residents. One was that, balconies should be
allowed in all houses. The second was that an additional room at the backside of the house should
be permitted because the family size has increased. The request for lower cantilever on the front
side of all houses has been accepted. But the demand for cantilever on the backside was not found
acceptable for certain reasons like privacy and technical reasons also. The second demand has been
accepted and notified. Recently, through a notification, a uniform policy throughout the city has
been adopted and there is no discrimination among the sectors, so far as height and other facilities
allowed in the basement are concerned. Discretionary powers from the lower official up to the level
of administrator has been done away with.
21.6 Responding to Mani Majra issue, the Finance Secretary elaborated that the issue did not
confine to Mani Majra alone but to the whole city. In response to a PIL the Hon’ble Punjab and
Haryana High Court had passed an order that all schools working from residential areas must be
stopped. Since it was practically not possible hence the deadline for shifting the school was fixed
as 31st March, 2006 and further extended to 31st March, 2007. Most of the schools have shifted
from the existing residential area to new sites. Some of the sites are under construction. He also
stated that second shift has been introduced in schools to accommodate greater number of
students.
21.7 The Committee appreciates the ambitious programme of U.T Administration of
Chandigarh to rehabilitate the slum dwellers by constructing dwelling units and giving them
on rent for Rs. 800 to Rs. 1,000 per month. Even though the Finance Secretary has stated
that the rent is a very reasonable amount which they will be paying and that their monthly
income is around Rs. 3,000 to Rs. 4000 per month, the Committee is apprehensive about
the capacity of the slum dwellers to pay Rs. 1,000 per month as rent. The Committee,
therefore, feels that this aspect may be taken care of. The Committee also desires that the
construction of units may be started and completed at the earliest so that shifting of slum
dwellers may also be done as early as possible. The target of three years for completing the
construction may strictly be adhered to.

42
21.8 In regard to technology park started in Chandigarh, the Committee is happy to note
that much progress has already taken place in setting up of the park and already 1,000
engineers have started working there. Several companies have already been allotted land.
This technology park is the only park of its kind in the Northern India and the Committee
recommends that all efforts may be made to ensure that the Technology Park is completed
in all respects at the earliest.
21.9 In regard to closure of schools in the residential areas of Chandigarh, the
Committee feels that the issue has become very sensitive in view of the fact that it is likely
to affect the future of many students. Even though the Finance Secretary has informed the
Committee that the second shift has been started in some of the schools to accommodate
the students from the closed schools, all the students will not get admission in such second
shifts. The Cemmittee, therefore, recommends that the Chandigarh Administration should
not allow this to happen and ensure that every student from all such closed schools may
be immediately provided admission in the existing schools by opening second shift and/or
increasing the class strength  whichever is necessary. The Chandigarh Administration should
also impress upon the managements of the closed schools to start their schools in the new
campuses as early as possible. The Chandigarh Administration may regularly monitor the
situation and find a lasting solution to this problem.

23.3 In the me eting of the Committee held on 4 April, 2007, the Chairperson observed that the
UTs of Daman and Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have been allocated only one-third of their total
budgetary demand, and desired to know as to what extent the projects, plans and programmes have
been affected due to resource crunch.
23.4 The Committee was informed that the Plan size for the Annual Plan 2007-08 for Daman and
Diu has been fixed at Rs. 70.88 crore which is quite insufficient to meet the requirements of the
Territory. Their minimum fund requirement for 2007-08 is Rs. 190 crore. Similarly, the Plan
size for the Annual Plan 2007-08 in respect of Dadra and Nagar Haveli has been fixed at
Rs.77.78 crore as against the minimum requirement of Rs. 232 crore. In regard to both the Union
Territories, it was also stated that with the passage of time, their requirement both on social sector,
social welfare and urban development have grown manifold. Growing requirement of social and
physical infrastructure needs higher allocation. It was also stated that if fund is not allocated, they
would neither be only able to service existing capital assets nor would they be able to create new
assets which are needed to meet the growing requirement.
23.5 The Administrator, during the course of his oral evidence, informed the Committee that the
Planning Commission did not hold any discussion with the Administrations of both the Union
Territories for Annual Plan allocations. He also informed that discussions were not held even for
the Eleventh Plan. He further informed the Committee that if discussions had taken place, they
would have informed the Planning Commission about the difficulties faced by them and about the
fund requirement.
23.6 The Committee is constrained to note that both the Union Territories of Daman and
Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have been getting very less grant as compared to the
projections made by them. In fact, Dadra and Nagar Haveli has been given about one-third
of the projected amount whereas Daman and Diu has been given less than 50 per cent of
the projected amount. With this reduction in the allocations, the activities proposed to be
taken up by the Union Territories would be considerably affected. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the allocations for both the Union Territories may be
increased appropriately at RE level. The Ministry of Home Affairs may also hold discussions
with the Planning Commission about the necessity of the projects proposed to be taken up
by the Union Territories. The Committee also recommends that the priority areas of
activities proposed to be taken up during 2007-08 may be completed as per the targets fixed.
Energy sector is an important area in which both the Union Territories proposed to set up

new sub-stations. Dadra and Nagar Haveli also proposes to augment the capacity of a sub-
station and Daman and Diu proposes to convert overhead lines to underground lines. These
activities may be undertaken on a priority basis and completed as per the targets fixed.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
CIVIC ACTION PROGRAMME OF BORDER GUARDING FORCES
The Committee feels that Civic Action Programme in the border areas is a very
important task. If undertaken well, it will infuse confidence among the border area
populace, develop infrastructure there and promote the feeling of national integration. For
all these to happen, the people should have confidence in the persons who are undertaking
such activities. However, people are sceptical about the uniformed personnel. The
Committee therefore recommends that the implementation of Civic Action Programme by
the BGFs need to be re-looked in its entirety. (Para 8.7)
RELIEF AND REHABILITATION MEASURES FOR J&K MIGRANTS
The Ministry of Home Affairs stated before the Committee that as it is a
reimbursement scheme, as soon as proposals for rehabilitation are received from the State
Government, the grants are provided accordingly. The Ministry further stated that the
schemes were not forthcoming from the State of J&K. As a result of this, though migrants
are living in sub-human conditions in rehabilitation camps, funds allocated for that purpose
are not utilised fully. In view of this, the Committee in its 119th Report had recommended
that Government should impress upon the J&K Government to come forward with schemes
in time and implement them without delay. But inspite of this, the Committee is disturbed
to learn that against the BE 2006-07 provision of Rs. 120 crore the expenditure during 2006-
07 is expected to be only Rs. 70 crore. The Committee once again strongly urges upon the
Ministry to further impress upon the J&K Government about the necessity of sending
schemes expeditiously and implement them in time so that all the J&K migrants are
rehabilitated without further delay. (Para 9.2)
COASTAL SECURITY SCHEME
The Committee feels that as there is a greater risk of infiltration from coastal belts,
the scheme needs to be implemented in the right earnest. This requires co-operation of all
the States. However, the Committee is constrained to note that some of the States have not
yet sanctioned the manpower. The Ministry may impress upon the State Governments
concerned to take early action in the matter. The Committee also recommends that the
process of acquiring boats may be completed at the earliest, as they are an essential
component for coastal security surveillance. In regard to the request of some State
Governments to the Centre to meet manpower cost, the Centre may hold consultations and
take a final view in the matter at the earliest. (Para 10.4)
NATIONAL DISASTER MANAGEMENT AUTHORITY
The Committee is constrained to note that the Rules relating to National Disaster
Response Force (NDRF) have not yet been notified. These rules are very essential for the
functioning of the Force. The Committee desires that the Rules may be finalised and
notified at the earliest. (Para 11.7)
50

51
Similarly, the Committee also expresses its concern over the slow pace in the
formulation of National Policy on Disaster Management. The Committee takes a strong
exception on the delay and recommends that Government should finalise the policy at the
earliest. (Para 11.8)
The Committee feels that a lot of work is still to be completed in regard to setting
up of Tsunami Warning System. The Committee recommends that all the necessary steps
may be taken for an expeditious setting up of Tsunami warning system. Steps may also be
taken for establishing the Central Receiving Station at New Delhi and parallel connectivity
at INCOIS, Hyderabad. (Para 11.10)
The Committee has also been informed that the Disaster Response Fund and
Disaster Mitigation Fund have not so far been constituted. It shows the lax attitude of the
Ministry in constituting such important funds for which the legislation was passed in 2005
itself. The Committee disapproves of this laxity and recommends that steps may be taken
for immediate constitution of the funds. (Para 11.11)
REVAMPING OF CIVIL DEFENCE
The Committee while commenting on the issue in its 119th and 124th Reports has
observed that the implementation of the revamping of Civil Defence has been tardy and
taking unduly long time. It is understandable that Government wants to have the views of
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) as the said scheme was to be integrated
in Disaster Management. But the Committee is at a loss to understand about consultations
being held now with State Governments which could have been done when the scheme was
conceived and formulated. Now it is causing unnecessary delays. The Committee, therefore,
recommends again to expedite the process of consultation with States and set a time limit
so that the scheme may take off this year. (Para 12.3)
INDIA-BANGLADESH BORDER FENCING WORKS
The Committee takes a serious note of the fact that the allocations are not being
spent. Besides the Ministry are also likely to take up Phase-ill of the fencing work. The
Committee strongly recommends that the physical and financial targets may be achieved
well in time and Phase-II may be completed at the earliest so that Phase-III may be
commenced as soon as possible. (Para 13.7)
The Committee is very much concerned about the problems being faced by the people
residing at the Border areas. It is a fact that there are properties of the Border people
where agricultural activities are carried out and in some areas, people are also residing in
this 150-yard of area. The Committee is anguished to note that people face lot of problems
under the current dispensation and no solution has been found so far for this problem. The
Committee recommends that the Government may hold discussion with Bangladesh in
consultation with the Ministry of External Affairs for a settlement of the problem. In
consultation with all concerned, the fencing may be taken nearer to the border instead of
150 yards away from the border. In case it is not possible the Government may buy the land
within this 150-yard of the Border so that the people who have properties within the 150
yards may not face problems any more. The Ministry of Home Affairs may hold discussions
with all concerned, including the Ministry of External Affairs and find a permanent solution
at the earliest. (para 13.9)
NAXALISM
The Committee notes that the Government are taking steps on different fronts

52
including the developmental efforts. The Committee has also recommended in successive
reports for a holistic approach in tackling the naxal problem. The Committee however, feels
that there is no perceptible change on the socio-economic front. Though the socio-economic
development cannot be quantified, it can be perceived and if such a perceptible change is
there, undoubtedly it will have a lasting impact. The Committee reiterating the earlier
recommendation that an effective developmental approach may be adopted, further
recommends that various schemes under the Ministries of Rural Development and other
Ministries may also be implemented for the socio-economic development in the naxal
affected areas. There needs to be an effective monitoring mechanism on the implementation
of these schemes with the involvement of all the concerned Ministries and agencies.
(Para 14.5)
The Committee also reiterates its observation made earlier that the naxal problem
is no longer a problem of a few States. It has acquired a national dimension posing gravest
threat to the national security. The naxal activities have spread to more than twelve States
and are reported to be having links with external agencies including ISI. The Committee
is therefore, of the considered view that taking into account the growth and influence of
the Naxal groups in several States and the grave threat posed by it to the internal security
of the country, it is high time that the Ministry constitute a Unified Command to effectively
tackle the menace. Besides the Central Paramilitary Forces, State Police Forces may also
contribute to the unified command. The Committee also takes note of the observation made
by the Home Secretary that naxal attacks on several occasions take place due to non
observance of ‘Standard Operating Procedure’ (SOP) by the state police forces. The
Committee therefore, strongly recommends that Government may consider creating a
unified command common to all the naxal affected States. (Para 14.6)
The Committee agrees that naxal threat is a big menace for any industry, including
the private sector. The issue needs to be examined to see that private sector industries are
also protected in the naxal-affected areas. The Ministry of Home Affairs may examine the
matter in consultation with all concerned and take an early decision. (Para 14.8)
MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCES
The Committee takes note of the Mid-Term evaluation of the Modernisation of State
Police Forces Scheme by BPR&D. One of the findings made by the BPR&D in the Study
which causes concern to the Committee is that more than 50 per cent of the fund is utilized
in the police housing and police building activities. The Committee is of the view that with
the new technological advances taking place in a feverish pitch and in view of the fact that
the Police Forces in India function with age-old equipments and gadgets, much of the
scheme of modernization should concentrate on providing modern gadgets, improving
technology, providing IT facilities, etc. Spending more than 50 per cent on building activities
defeats the very purpose of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends
that the Ministry of Home Affairs may review the scheme in the light of pattern of
expenditure incurred by the States and prepare a list of activities which should lay thrust
on improving technology and providing modern gadgets, etc. (Para 15.6)
The Committee is constrained to note that there was an unspent balance of Rs. 47.81
crore under the Scheme of Modernisation of Police forces as on 31.12.2006. Though the
Ministry have stated that they are pursuing vigorously with the States for better and full
utilization of funds, the Committee desires that they may lay a condition stating that
further funds would be released only after the full expenditure of the previous balance. It
should be insisted upon all the States to send Utilisation Certificates and receipt thereof

53
may also be put as one of the conditions for further release of funds. These are necessary
to ensure that States spend the funds meant for Modernization of Police Forces in a better
manner and as per the schedule. (Para 15.7)
The Committee notes with satisfaction launching of the scheme of Modernisation of
Police Forces in UTs. Since it was initiated in 2006-07 only, it would be too early to assess
the scheme. The Committee notes that UTs were asked in 2006-07 to implement this
scheme effectively by having savings. Though ultimately additional allocation had to be
made as UTs could not effect savings, such a situation could have been avoided by making
allocation initially which would have enabled the UTs to start implementation immediately.
The Ministry may therefore from time-to-time monitor the implementation of the scheme
and ensure that the physical as well as financial target are achieved in time by the State
and Union Territories. (Para 15.10)
The Committee is given to understand that Special Branches in States/UTs Police
Forces play an important role in collection of intelligence through technical surveillance and
the real and actionable intelligence at the micro-level comes through human assets.
However, the Committee is of the view that the Special Branches neither have sufficient
infrastructure nor modern equipment and gadgets, etc. In view of the current internal
security situation and the growing naxalite and terrorist activities, strengthening and
modernization of Special Branches acquire significance. The Committee, therefore, feels
that the Special Branches in the States/Union Territories Police Forces need to be revamped
by enhancing their manpower by way of filling up of vacancies; posting of competent officers
with reasonable tenure, dedicated staff for intelligence work right up to the police station
level and reactivating beat constable system and above all making available modern
equipment and gadgets for interception and special training for personnel posted therein.
(Para 15.11)
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may
impress upon the State/Union Territories Governments/Administrations to strengthen their
Special Branches. The Ministry may also allocate some of the funds under Modernization of
States Polices Forces Scheme for strengthening and modernization of Special Branches.
(Para 15.12)
MODERNISATION OF PRISON ADMINISTRATION
The Committee reiterates its observation made in its 119th Report that the Scheme,
if implemented in the right earnest, would go a long way in improving the conditions in the
prisons and the inmates thereof. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that more
emphasis is laid under the Scheme on the construction work, repairs and renovation than
improving the actual conditions inside the jails for the prisoners. The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that the Government may redesign the guidelines for the scheme
laying more emphasis on improving the facilities/conditions of the prisoners. (Para 16.5)
The Committee also expresses its concern that even though the Scheme started in
2002-2003, no evaluation of its performance has been made so far. The Ministry’s reply that
a study evaluation is normally carried out after completion of the scheme shows a casual
approach of dealing with the matter. Whenever any scheme is launched a mid-term
evaluation is carried out. Since the scheme has been extended by two more years with effect
from 01.04.2007, the Government may conduct a mid-term evaluation immediately to assess
its efficacy. (Para 16.6)

54
The Committee is presently examining the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment)
Bill, 2006. One of the provisions in the Bill seeks to amend Section 167 of the Code for
allowing video conferencing between the Jail and the Court for trial of an accused to avoid
transportation of the accused to the court. To make this provision workable it is essential
to modernise the jails, especially enabling those with IT facilities, computers and all related
equipments. Most of the jails in the country do not have this facility at present. In case,
the above-mentioned amendment is enacted, it would practically be of no use unless the
required infrastructure is available in the jails. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
creation of infrastructure in the jails for enabling video linkages between the jails and the
courts, may be made part of the scheme of Modernisation of Prisons and if necessary a
separate allocation may be made for that purpose. (Para 16.7)
SCHEME FOR POLICE HOUSING
Housing for Central Police Forces (CPFs) personnel
The Committee is constrained to note that the Plan Allocation approved by the
Planning Commission for the Tenth Five Year Plan of Rs.I037.50 crore was reduced to
Rs. 729 crore. The originally projected expenditure for the Tenth Plan by the Ministry was
Rs.10,000 crore. The Committee desires that the Planning Commission may make a realistic
assessment of the requirement of the scheme and make allocations accordingly. Had the
projected expenditure of Rs. 2,000 crore under Plan and Non-Plan been spent during the
Tenth Plan, the satisfaction level of Twenty five per cent would have been achieved. Due to
reduction in allocation, that satisfaction level may have gone down drastically. The
Committee desires that at least twenty percent satisfaction level in all the States needs to
be achieved for which necessary allocation may be made. The Committee also recommends
that the Government may commission a review of the implementation of the scheme with
a view to critically analyse its implementation. (Para 17.3)
Housing for Delhi Police Personnel
The Committee is unhappy to note that none of the housing projects on hand of the
Delhi Police has taken off so far. The project at Dwarka could not commence due to
increase in plinth area/covered area as per requirement of Delhi Urban Arts Commission.
The Committee feels that the outstanding issues should have been sorted out before the
project was approved. Now that the tenders have already been invited for starting the
construction work, the Committee recommends that the physical targets may be adhered to.
(Para 17.7)
The Committee expresses its concern that even after three years of allotment of
land at Mandoli, the construction has not started. It is very strange that the issue of land
use is being considered now after three years of allotment of land. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry may intervene in the matter and get the clearance from DDA
at the earliest so that construction of the flats may commence without further delay.
(Para 17.8)
REPEALING OF OBSOLETE ACTS
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may have a fresh look at
these laws and bring them in line with the present times. The Committee also recommends
that the obsolete laws need to be repealed from time to time and this should be
appropriately included in the Action Plan of the Ministry. (Para 18.1)

55
ACQUIRING OF WEAPONS BY SPORTSPERSONS
The Committee feels that use of advanced and imported weapons is essential for
shooters who participate in national and international championships. To enable the shooters
to excel in international events, it is necessary for the Government to allow them to import
advanced weapons. The Government may consider all the aspects relating to permission for
acquiring of imported weapons by the shooters and take an early decision in the matter. The
Committee also suggests that the sportspersons, so permitted to acquire imported weapons,
may also be permitted to dispose them of after every three years as the use of the weapons
may involve wear and tear and technological changes may make it obsolete. (Para 19.3)
UNION TERRITORIES WITHOUT LEGISLATURE
Demand No. 94 – Andaman and Nicobar Islands
The Committee feels that though an elaborate thinking has gone into the planning and
construction of permanent shelters, the delay in completion of the construction is cause of
concern. The allocation of shelters should be completed as per the targets. The Committee
also feels that the action plan prepared for improving tourism, particularly involving private
sector is the need of the hour. The action plan may be implemented immediately.  (Para 20.18)
The Committee also understands that the Island Administration has a proposal of
procurement of two fixed wing aircrafts and two helicopters which is held up in Ministry of
Civil Aviation. The Ministry of Civil Aviation may clear the proposal at the earliest. The
Ministry of Home Affairs may also consult the Ministry of Civil Aviation for an early
clearance of the proposal. (Para 20.19)
Demand No. 95 - Chandigarh
The Committee appreciates the ambitious programme of U.T Administration of
Chandigarh to rehabilitate the slum dwellers by constructing dwelling units and giving them
on rent for. Rs. 800 to Rs. 1,000 per month. Even though the Finance Secretary has stated
that the rent is a very reasonable amount which they will be paying and that their monthly
income is around Rs. 3,000 to Rs. 4000 per month, the Committee is apprehensive about
the capacity of the slum dwellers to pay Rs. 1,000 per month as rent. The Committee,
therefore, feels that this aspect may be taken care of. The Committee also desires that the
construction of units may be started and completed at the earliest so that shifting of slum
dwellers may also be done as early as possible. The target of three years for completing the
construction may strictly be adhered to. (Para 21.7)
In regard to technology park started in Chandigarh, the Committee is happy to note
that much progress has already taken place in setting up of the park and already 1,000
engineers have started working there. Several companies have already been allotted land.
This technology park is the only park of its kind in the Northern India and the Committee
recommends that all efforts may be made to ensure that the Technology Park is completed
in all respects at the earliest. (Para 21.8)
In regard to closure of schools in the residential areas of Chandigarh, the
Committee feels that the issue has become very sensitive in view of the fact that it is likely
to affect the future of many students. Even though the Finance Secretary has informed the
Committee that the second shift has been started in some of the schools to accommodate
the students from the closed schools, all the students will not get admission in such second
shifts. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Chandigarh Administration should
not allow this to happen and ensure that every student from all such closed schools may
be immediately provided admission in the existing schools by opening second. shift and/or

56
increasing the class strength whichever is necessary. The Chandigarh Administration should
also impress upon the managements of the closed schools to start their schools in the new
campuses as early as possible. The Chandigarh Administration may regularly monitor the
situation and find a lasting solution to this problem. (Para 21.9)
Demand No. 96 – Dadra and Nagar Haveli; and
Demand No. 97 – Daman and Diu
The Committee is constrained to note that both the Union Territories of Daman and
Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have been getting very less grant as compared to the
projections made by them. In fact, Dadra and Nagar Haveli has been given about one-third
of the projected amount whereas Daman and Diu has been given less than 50 per cent of
the projected amount. With this reduction in the allocations, the activities proposed to be
taken up by the Union Territories would be considerably affected. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the allocations for both the Union Territories may be
increased appropriately at RE level. The Ministry of Home Affairs may also hold discussions
with the Planning Commission about the necessity of the projects proposed to be taken up
by the Union Territories. The Committee also recommends that the priority areas of
activities proposed to be taken up during 2007-08 may be completed as per the targets fixed.
Energy sector is an important area in which both the Union Territories proposed to set up
new sub-stations. Dadra and Nagar Hayeli, also proposes to augment the capacity of a sub-
station and Daman and Diu proposes to convert overhead lines to underground lines. These
activities may be undertaken on a priority basis and completed as per the targets fixed.
(Para 23.6)
Demand No. 98 – Lakshadweep
The Administrator, Lakshadweep, during the course of his oral evidence before the
Committee, stated that though the Plan Allocation has increased from Rs.209 crore
at RE 2006-07 to Rs.222.11 crore in BE 2007-08, it was way below the projection of
Rs. 402 crore made by the Lakshadweep Administration before the Planning Commission.
The main reason for projecting Rs.402 crore was that the growth rate during the Tenth Five
Year Plan had become very fast and they wanted to maintain that tempo. He further stated
that discussions were held with the Planning Commission but they were told that the outer
limit of the allocation would be Rs.222 crore only though they appreciated the presentation
made by the Administration. (Para 24.3)
The Committee feels that the allocation made is too meagre as compared to the
projections made by the Lakshadweep Administration in view of the necessity of sustaining
the tempo of the growth rate. The Planning Commission may consider increasing the
allocation to a reasonable extent at RE level so that Lakshadweep may go ahead with its
planned activities. This is necessary because Lakshadweep has a large potential for tourism
and unless adequate infrastructure is created, tourism cannot improve. (Para 24.4)
Among the priority sectors proposed to be taken up during the current financial
year, implementation of perspective plan for shipping sector is an important one. Ships,
ferries, landing barges, oil barges, etc., are proposed to be acquired besides two helicopters.
The Committee endorses the proposal for taking up shipping sector as a priority area during
2007-08 and all the proposed activities may be completed as targeted. (Para 24.5)
Necessary steps may be taken to implement the proposal for opening all islands
for tourism and open up public-private participation in tourism, so that tourism may develop
as a major activity in the islands which has the potential to provide employment.
(Para 24.6)

3.2 While making a presentation on the Civic Action Programme of the Border Guarding Forces

62
etc. The Home Secretary during the course of the presentation has stated that out of 73 police

Some State Governments have objected to this because on the other side of the fencing, there are

Secretary explaining the reason for this condition of 150 yards away from the Border stated that
there was an unsigned agreement since 1975 between Bangladesh and India. The unsigned
agreement was that for 150 yards, there would be no defence structure. Though’ fencing’ is not

yards of the Border. It was also agreed that because of this condition, a large number of villages

surveillance equipments have been supplied to them. Forty per cent recruitment in the Central
Paramilitary Forces was expected to be from the border areas and areas affected by militancy with

of the naxal affected States do not found to have sufficient force system. Certain States have a
large number of vacancies in their force. One of the State has about 10,000 vacancies. He further
stated that there is a limit upto which the CPMFs can help the States forces but they can not
completely substitute the State Police Forces and the Ministry was impressing upon the States to
fill up the vacancies on priority basis. The Home Secretary has also sated that the States Police

attack by the naxals.

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
OVERVIEW
The States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura
and Sikkim having rich natural resources with fertile land, dense forests and substantive mineral
and hydrocarbon deposits form part of North-Eastern Region of the country. With a view to
convert the untapped potential of North Eastern Region into an opportunity, the policy of the
Central Government inter alia focuses on special assistance to upgrade and expand infrastructure
and accords priority to the development and expansion of physical infrastructure like roads,
highways, power, water supply etc. In this direction the Ministry of Development of North-Eastern
Region (DoNER) was formed as a Department in September 2001 and then was upgraded to
the status of a Ministry in May, 2004. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business)
Rules, 1961, the Ministry of DoNER is concerned with the following:
(i) Matters relating to the planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes
and projects of North Eastern Region including those in the sectors of Power,
Irrigation, Roads and Communications;
(ii) Hill Area Development Programme and Border Area Development Programme in North
Eastern Region;*
(iii) Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources for North Eastern Region (NLCPR);
(iv) North Eastern Council (NEC);
(v) North East Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi);
(vi) North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited (NERAMAC);
(vii) Sikkim Mining Corporation Limited (SMC);
(viii) North Eastern Handloom and Handicrafts Development Corporation (NEHHDC);
(ix) Road works fina nced in whole or in part by the Central Government in the North
Eastern Region; and
(x) Planning of Road and Inland Waterways Transport in the North Eastern Region.
2.0 The Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region seeks to achieve the following goals:
* Accelerating the pace of socio-economic development in the North Eastern Region.
* Synergizing the efforts of Central/State Governments/Other Stakeholders for balanced
development of the Region.
* Integrated and holistic planning for the region, taking into account the heightened
consciousness of the people of the reigon, their aspiration, needs and sensitivities.
* Evolving a common approach for all the agencies working for the development of the
region.
* Included in the original mandate of the Ministry of DoNER but has not been transferred from Planning
Commission and MHA, respectively.

2
* Formulating appropriate policies for the rapid development of the region.
3.0 The North Eastern Council (NEC) , Shillong, an organization under the Ministry, is the
Regional Planning Body for the region. It was set up under the NEC Act, 1971 for securing the
balanced development of the North East. The Minister in charge of the Ministry of Development of
North Eastern Region is ex-officio Chairman of NEC. Its Members include the Governors and the
Chief Ministers of the eight Member States and three Members nominated by the President of India.
4.0 In the Tenth Plan period, the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER)
had been implementing the following Central Plan Schemes:
* Advocacy and Publicity,
* Technical Assistance and Capacity Building,
* Assistance to Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC),
* Assistance to North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi).
4.1 However, under the Plan allocation for 2007-08, Planning Commission has transferred a
scheme, Development of Inland Waterways” in North East, to this Ministry under the Central Plan
Scheme from Department of Shipping, Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways. On
the other hand, SMC has been dropped from the Central Plan scheme w.e.f. 2007-08 as a decision
has been taken to wind up the Corporation.
5.0 The Ministry implements the work mandated in Allocation of Business Rules, 1961, through
the formulation of appropriate policies, and implementation of specific Plan Programmes. The North
Eastern Council, Shillong also implements various Plan Schemes in the region.
6.0 Besides the above, the following Schemes are also under implementation in the form of
Assistance to the State Plans:
* Non-Iapsable Central Pool of Resources for North Eastern Region (NLCPR)
* Plan Schemes of the North Eastern Council (NEC)
* Infrastructure development projects under the special package for Bodoland Territorial
Council
* Development of Cities and Roads in the North Eastern States (Externally Aided
Projects)
6.1 Since 1998-99, all non-exempted Ministries/Departments of Government of India are
required to earmark at least 10% of their Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for the development of
North Eastern States for creation of both economic and social infrastructure such as Power, Roads
and Bridges, Education, Health, Water Supply and Sanitation etc. in the region. The unutilized
portion of the 10% Plan allocation made by Ministries/Departments is credited at the end of each
financial year in a Reserve fund in the Public Account titled ‘Central Resource Pool for
Development of North Eastern Region’ and is known as the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of
Resources (NLCPR). The funds from this Pool are budgeted for financing new infrastructure
projects/schemes in the region under the NLCPR Plan Scheme.
6.2 The NLCPR is run for infrastructure development in almost all the major socio-economic
development sectors. For this purpose, projects are sanctioned for State sector as well as Central
sector projects/schemes. However, the funds available under the Central Pool are not meant to
supplement the normal Plan programmes either of the State Governments or Union Ministries/
Departments/Agencies.

3
7.0 The Ministry also supervises the work of two Public Sector Undertakings, viz., North
Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Ltd. (NEHHDC), North Eastern
Regiona1 Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. (NERAMAC).
8.0 While the respective Ministries/Departments are responsible in respect of subjects allocated
to them, the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region coordinates with various Ministries/
Departments of Government of India and the State Governments for various development and
welfare programmes/schemes/activities in North Eastern Region. In that direction, every week,
Secretary holds meetings with the officers of one of the Ministries and the concerned officers of
the State Governments.
9.0 To review the progress of Central Sector/Centrally Sponsored Schemes being implemented
by Central Ministries/Departments and also with a view to evolve policy framework for each sector
and also to ensure that maximum development takes place in the North-East Region, 16 sector-
specific high level meetings chaired by Minister, DoNER have been fixed for every month by
rotation in the Capitals and some other important towns of the eight North-East States.

NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
12.0 Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) has been created by the Government of
India for the States of North Eastern Region out of the unspent amount of stipulated ten percent
of Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) of individual Ministries/Departments of Government of India for
financing infrastructural development projects in the North-East. However, at present, eighteen
Ministries/Departments have been exempted for allocating the stipulated ten percent of GBS for NE
States.
12.1 The Ministry in their written reply on the grounds on which eighteen Ministries/
Departments, particularly Petroleum and Natural Gas, Social Justice and Empowerment have been
exempted from allocating the stipulated ten percent of Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for the NE
States stated that the following criteria are being followed for exempting a Ministry/Department
from earmarking 10% of their GBS for the North East:—

7
(a) Highly scientific Ministries/Departments with hardly any scope for work in the
North East;
(b) The Ministries/Departments having no direct involvement in the North East including
Sikkim such as the erstwhile Department of Ocean Development;
(c) The Ministries in which case the expenditure in the North Eastern Region was
‘Nil’ during the last three years; and
Government of India does not provide any Budgetary Support to Ministry of Petroleum and
Natural Gas, as the Ministry generates its own resources. The Ministry is therefore
exempted from making provisions to North East. As regards Ministry of Social Justice and
Empowerment, all Divisions of the Ministry other than the Scheduled Castes Division (SCD)
do earmark 10% of their Plan allocations to the North Eastern region. In the case of the
Scheduled Castes Division, only 2% of its GBS is allocated to the North East (NE),
considering the fact that the Scheduled Castes constitute less than 2% of the NE population.
12.2 The Secretary, Ministry of DoNER in her presentation informed the Committee that
consequent to the recommendation of the Committee in its 120th Report to review the exempted
Ministries, a review of exempted Ministries was carried out and exemption to Department of
Biotechnology was withdrawn. She added that guidelines to administer NLCPR were formulated in
December, 2001 and revised in July, 2004 to make them more comprehensive and that further
additional provisions were made in February 2007. An Inter ministerial Committee headed by
Secretary DONER has been constituted to administer NLCPR funded schemes. States are required
to submit priority list of socio-economic infrastructure projects with concept papers for such
projects by 31st December. Thereafter the Committee considers the list and selects appropriate
projects and after approval of Minister, DoNER the States are requested to submit Detailed Project
Reports (DPRs) of the selected projects. DPRs are examined in consultation with the Ministries of
Government of India and the proposals are put up before the Committee whose recommendations
are submitted for approval of Minister. She mentioned that eight hundred and forty two projects
worth Rs. 5,967.97 crore have been approved and Rs. 4,358.77 crore released to the States up
to 31 March, 2007.
12.2.1 Elaborating upon the monitoring of projects, the Secretary stated that rigorous monitoring
through Quarterly Progress Reports is done and funds are released only after certified utilization
of earlier releases. Progress is reviewed with the state authorities periodically. She further
mentioned that recently a system of online data entry has been introduced and monthly reviews
through video conference have started. Concerned officers of the State Governments are also
required to inspect projects regularly.
